A spokesperson for Reform said: “Reform UK has been the target of a hoax ‌perpetrated by foreign-funded, climate change activists posing as would-be party donors. The ⁠party denies any wrongdoing.
“Reform UK has a robust vetting process for prospective donors approved by the Electoral Commission.”
The Metropolitan Police said ⁠it was aware of the allegations in the broadcast and would assess any information provided to them. This did not amount to the formal launch of an investigation.

The Electoral Commission, which oversees ‌and regulates political finance in Britain, said: “We are ​considering all relevant information, in line with our regulatory remit, and we are ‌in touch with the Met Police.
“The Electoral Commission has not ​approved the donor vetting process for Reform, or any other party. Parties are responsible for ensuring their internal processes and controls are fit for purpose.”

title: In Nepal, mourners hold symbolic cremation for missing loved ones
summary: As hopes for those still missing fade, families without the remains of their relatives are burning effigies on miniature funeral pyres.
story: The wall of ice, water and rock that tore through Nepal last week has claimed more than 1,200 lives and left more than 4,000 missing, depriving many grieving families of a basic rite: funerals.

The scale of the disaster has proved challenging for authorities, with morgues overwhelmed by a large number of unidentified remains. In many cases, bodies have been washed far downstream and rendered unrecognizable, while others still missing are feared to have been buried in the torrent of thick mud.
As hopes fade that survivors will be found, a week on from the disaster, family members without the remains of their loved ones have begun to hold symbolic cremations.
The ceremonies provide an outlet for the grief and uncertainty that have gripped so many in Nepal, and ensure that a key religious rite is afforded to the dead.

At Kathmandu’s Pashupatinath Temple, the most revered Hindu temple in Nepal, mourners gathered Wednesday to mark the loss of missing loved ones. On the banks of the holy Bagmati River, they burned effigies made of kusa grass, also called darbha, a plant used in Hindu rituals, on miniature funeral pyres.
The small stick figures, wrapped in orange cloth, were rubbed in paste and covered in garlands of orange flowers.

title: Iran targets American bases after U.S. strikes sites near Strait of Hormuz
summary: The strikes were in “retaliation for the Iranians’ failed attempt at adding sea mines” in the Strait of Hormuz, Trump said on Truth Social.
story: TEHRAN, Iran — Hostilities between the United States and Iran escalated overnight into Wednesday, with Tehran attacking American bases across the Middle East after a U.S. strike was alleged to have hit a home hosting a wedding event, killing five and wounding dozens.

President Donald Trump said in a post on Truth Social Tuesday that the U.S. had launched a wave of “large and powerful” strikes on Iranian targets near the Strait of Hormuz in retaliation for what he said was a “failed attempt” at laying mines along the vital trade route.
Trump told reporters at the Oval Office on Wednesday that the U.S. military could attack again.
“It was a very heavy attack last night, and we’re prepared to do another one any time we want,” he said.

U.S. Central Command, or CENTCOM, said Tuesday it had carried out attacks on Iranian military targets, including air defense sites, radar systems, maritime assets and facilities, communication sites and mine-laying capabilities.

The Iranian Red Crescent later said five people had been killed and nearly 70 injured after a U.S. strike hit what it called a “wedding celebration” in the city of Kuhestak, on the Strait of Hormuz, according to the semiofficial Fars news agency. The regional Red Crescent said at least one child was among those killed.
NBC News was not immediately able to independently confirm the details of the strike.

In video published by the Iranian Red Crescent Society and geolocated to Kuhestak by NBC News, a building can be seen surrounded by rubble, with a gaping hole blown through its roof. Other footage appears to show a downed telecommunications tower just a few minutes’ walk away from the building.
CENTCOM spokesperson Navy Capt. Tim Hawkins said he was aware of reports of civilian casualties.
The “U.S. military never targets civilians, unlike the IRGC,” he said, referring to Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Corps.

In response, the IRGC said it had launched a wave of strikes targeting U.S. bases across the region, including in Iraq, the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain and Kuwait.  In a statement, the IRGC said the strikes were in retaliation to the U.S. bombing, which it described as a “flagrant violation of human rights” that turned what it described as an “engagement” event into a “mourning ceremony.”
The IRGC also said it had targeted bases in Jordan.
The Kuwaiti army said in a post on X early Thursday local time that it was defending against an attack.
“Kuwaiti Air Defenses are currently responding to hostile missile and drone threats,” the Kuwaiti army wrote in the post.

In a separate statement, the IRGC said that four members of its own aerospace forces were also killed in Kermanshah, a city in the central district of Kermanshah province, in U.S. strikes overnight, the semiofficial Tasnim news agency reported.
“Make no mistake: these crimes will not go unpunished,” Ebrahim Azizi, chairperson of the Iranian parliament’s National Security and Foreign Policy Committee, said on X.

If the Islamic Republic retaliates, Trump had warned, “they will be hit again at a much harder and higher level, but it will not be the biggest attack of them all, that is waiting in the wings.” When that is over, he added, “there will be very little left” of the country.
The latest bout of violence, which began on Sunday with an American bombing of a key island in the Strait of Hormuz, has ended a monthlong lull in fighting between the U.S. and Iran.

title: Nepal flood deaths pass 1,100 as hope fades in the search for survivors
summary: The overwhelming stench of death is crushing hopes that more survivors will be found in this Nepali town devastated by last week’s catastrophic floods.
story: BIDUR, Nepal — At the Nepal army staging area in the heart of the flood zone, the roar of helicopters overhead carrying flood aid mixes with the rumble of a bulldozer digging a mass grave.
The overwhelming stench of death is crushing hopes that more survivors will be found in Bidur, a town in Nepal’s Nuwakot district, devastated by last week’s catastrophic floods.
Workers in white hazmat suits unload bodies from a stream of ambulances. They place the wrapped bodies onto a blue tarp in a cordoned-off area.
Helicopters, both military and private aircraft that in better days would be used for commercial tours, take off packed with aid before returning with survivors in need of medical care.
Kalpana Shrestha, a nurse who works in the capital, Kathmandu, is desperate. Ten members of her family are missing — her two sisters and their three children.

“I have shared their photos with journalists, on social media and YouTube, but I have not got any response at all,” she told NBC News in Kathmandu on Tuesday. She added that her loved ones disappeared in Betrawati, a town some 60 miles from the capital that was obliterated in the flooding.
“I have posted so much that my fingers started shaking and trembling,” Shrestha, 35, said. “My mind has stopped working. But even so, we have not stopped posting.”

More than 1,114 have been declared dead in Nepal after last week’s devastating floods, according to Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority. Over 3,916 others are still missing, including at least 583 foreign nationals. In Tibet, at least 16 people were killed and 546 are missing, according to CGTN, China’s English-language satellite news channel.
A State Department spokesperson said Tuesday that 75 Americans remain unaccounted for and that 14 have made their way to safety in Nepal.
More than 10,000 people have been rescued so far, including 252 foreign nationals, the United Nations said.

The disaster, which was triggered by a glacier collapse and landslide on Nepal’s border with China, is now considered Nepal’s deadliest natural disaster since the April 2015 earthquake that killed around 9,000 people.

title: Thousands of U.S. service members arrive in Thailand after record stint at sea
summary: About 5,000 U.S. sailors and Marines are stopping in the resort city of Pattaya for a “rest and relaxation” break as they return home from a record-setting deployment in the Middle East.
story: LAEM CHABANG, Thailand — The USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier arrived Wednesday at a port in eastern Thailand, where thousands of U.S. sailors and Marines are disembarking for the first time in more than 280 days after a record-setting deployment in the Middle East.

The toll of the more than nine-month deployment, most of it spent supporting military operations in the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran, was visible on the carrier as it pulled into Laem Chabang Port in Chonburi province. Paint has worn off and the metal underneath is rusted on the 1,092-foot warship, which is one of the largest in the world.

The Lincoln is in Thailand for a four-day “rest and relaxation” stop on its way home to San Diego after having spent weeks in the headlines as the lengthy deployment raised concerns about supply shortages and the effect on sailors’ mental health.

The U.S. Navy confirmed the ship’s arrival in a statement, saying the Lincoln strike group arrived in Laem Chabang while the destroyer USS Frank E. Petersen Jr. docked in nearby Sriracha and the guided-missile cruiser USS Robert Smalls went to Map Ta Phut in neighboring Rayong province.
The Navy said it was the Lincoln’s first full port stop after 286 days at sea since the deployment began in November.

“Our arrival in Laem Chabang provides a well-deserved opportunity for our sailors and Marines to rest and recharge,” said Rear Adm. Robert E. Loughran, commander of Carrier Strike Group 3. “It also underscores the strong and enduring partnership and alliance between the United States and Thailand.”

About 5,000 sailors and Marines are expected to hit the streets of Pattaya, a nearby coastal resort city that is one of the most popular tourist destinations in Thailand. Each service member will get three “liberty days” and one day of duty aboard the ship, a U.S. military official said.

Upon the Lincoln’s arrival in the morning, service members could be seen working aboard the deck as loudspeakers played announcements about the process for disembarkation. A whistle could be heard ringing across the deck, a Navy tradition that signals coming ashore.
Thai police crackdown on sex workers

Around 1 p.m. local time (2 a.m. ET), service members began disembarking from the ship in civilian clothes, some carrying backpacks. One service member was carrying his golf clubs. Waiting for them across the way were dozens of Ford pickup trucks and buses lined up in columns to take them into town.
“Please be on your best behavior,” a commanding officer could be heard saying over loudspeaker.

Locals in tourism-dependent Pattaya have eagerly awaited the arrival of the Lincoln, which pulled into sight from the shore after sunrise before it made a wide turn and harbored itself at a major cargo terminal.

Officials in Pattaya, where international tourist arrivals have dropped because of travel disruptions and soaring fuel prices stemming from the conflict in the Middle East, say the visit is expected to inject about $3 million into the local economy.

Authorities in Pattaya have stepped up security, with heightened police patrols and checks along the roads. Businesses here are also trying to woo the sailors, with some putting up banners to welcome them.
Wichai Yuankham, 35, a factory worker who came to watch the ships arrive, said the naval visit was a welcome boost to the local economy.
“I am just excited to see the destroyer docking,” he said. “This is my first time seeing the destroyer, and I feel good seeing it, and we can boast to our neighboring countries about this.”

title: Allies bristle as sanctioned Russian finance minister attends U.S.-hosted G20 summit
summary: Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov was left out of the “family photo” of finance ministers at a G20 meeting after complaints from Ukraine’s allies.
story: ASHEVILLE, N.C. — Traditionally the “family photo” of finance ministers at a G20 meeting is a dull, grimacing group clad mostly in gray. But this year’s picture may be much more interesting for some because of whom it omits.

Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov — who was sanctioned by the United States in April 2022 — was left out after complaints from some of Ukraine’s European allies as he attended his first Group of 20 summit on U.S. soil since President Vladimir Putin invaded his neighbor four years ago, NBC News has learned.

Having served in the role since 2011, Siluanov is widely considered to be one of Putin’s most trusted Cabinet members. But he was given the cold shoulder by some of those in attendance at the event in Asheville, North Carolina, although he addressed the summit and met with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.

Bessent told NBC News on Tuesday that he brought up “with everyone that we have implemented our economic outcast policy, and that we expect everyone to come along with us.” He was referring to sanctions he introduced last week targeting countries and international entities facilitating trade with Iran.
Asked about Siluanov’s response, Bessent said: “Many conversations are best done privately.”

But a source familiar with the meeting told NBC News on Monday that Bessent, who sanctioned Russia’s two largest oil companies in October,  had made clear to his counterpart the “U.S. will not provide Russia with economic relief until the war in Ukraine is over.”
When Siluanov tried to discuss areas of interest, Bessent “forcefully interrupted and said nothing is possible until the war is over,” the source added.

The pair met on the sidelines of the forum, with the discussion focusing on “Russian-American cooperation,” the Russian Finance Ministry said in a statement on its website. The ministry did not immediately react to NBC News’ request for comment about Siluanov’s omission from the “family photo.”

Siluanov’s presence appeared to rattle some of Ukraine’s European allies, including German Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil, who said the signal sent ​by ​receiving the ⁠Russian finance minister in the U.S. was “quite troubling.”

title: Record baby boom brings world’s heaviest parrot back from the brink
summary: A record 90 chicks have been added to the population count of the kakapo parrot in New Zealand, delighting conservationists.
story: There’s been a baby boom among one of the world’s most endangered parrot species — and officials in New Zealand are squawking about it.
A record 90 chicks have been added to the count of the endangered kakapo parrot, bringing the population to a record 325 birds, the New Zealand Conservation Department said in a statement Tuesday.

The fledglings of the bird, which is native to New Zealand, were bred this year. The youngest is now 150 days old, a milestone at which the baby birds are considered independent enough to be added to the tally.
And every bird counts.
The green parrots do not fly and have a waddling gait, making them an easy target for ground predators. The kakapo is also the heaviest parrot species, with males weighing up to 9 pounds.

The bright birds, with finely blotched yellow-green plumage and large gray beaks, are also thought to be among the longest‑living bird species, reaching 60 to 90 years, the statement from the department said.
The nocturnal parrots with their owl-like faces remain critically endangered, conservationists say.

“There is still a long road of recovery ahead, but ninety chicks in a single season is a record. In the early years of recovery, it took 16 years to produce that many chicks,” said Deidre Vercoe, manager of the department’s kakapo recovery operations.

“We had a four-year gap between breeding seasons, so it’s fantastic to finally see the population increase,” she said in a statement. “It’s also a significant milestone for the species, as the last time the population is thought to have exceeded 300 birds may have been as long as 75 years ago.”

The Kakapo Recovery Programme began in 1995 with a population of just 51 birds, including only 20 females. Since then, the species has been through 13 breeding seasons, with recovery efforts working to overcome challenges associated with low genetic diversity, including infertility and poor hatching success. The successful season also highlights the importance of creating more predator-free habitats for the species.
Each kakapo in the program is fitted with a small backpack radio transmitter to help track its location and monitor its activity levels, conservationists say.

title: Thieves steal royal necklace from Vienna museum in smash-and-grab heist
summary: The robbers, who didn’t disguise their faces and were caught on camera, remain at large with the 673-diamond necklace once owned by an Egyptian queen, police said.
story: Austrian police are searching for a pair of brazen thieves who made off with a diamond necklace — once owned by an Egyptian queen and worth millions — by smashing a display case at a Vienna museum in broad daylight.
But unloading the hot rocks stolen last week from the Museum of Applied Arts, known as MAK, could be their undoing, art heist experts said Monday.

“Just like with paintings, it’s hard to sell well-known pieces of jewelry,” said Anthony Amore, a Boston-based art theft expert and investigator. “The Catch-22 is nobody will buy it intact. So it would not surprise me if their aim is to take the piece apart and sell the jewels individually.”
Robert Wittman, who once led the FBI’s Art Crime Team and is now a security consultant, agreed.
“What I expect they aim to do is pop the diamonds out of the settings and melt it down,” he said.
If they do, they will dramatically reduce the value of a one-of-a-kind piece that Sotheby’s auction house in New York sold in 2015 for $4.3 million, the experts said.

“They’re better thieves than businessmen,” Wittman said. “What gives this piece its value is not just the diamonds, but the provenance, the history of the piece. They take this piece apart and they’ll be lucky to get a couple hundred thousand, if that.”
That’s if the thieves can find a buyer for the baubles, the experts said.
“Anybody who knows anything about diamonds is going to know where these diamonds came from,” Wittman said.

The robbery bore little resemblance to jewel heists depicted in movies like “The Thomas Crown Affair” or “Ocean’s 8.” The thieves didn’t scale the walls after hours or short-circuit the security system to get inside the museum.
Instead, according to police, they bought tickets, strolled in with their faces uncovered and made their way to an exhibition of works from the French luxury jeweler Van Cleef & Arpels.

There, the 200-carat platinum necklace encrusted with 673 diamonds, which once belonged to Queen Consort Nazli of Egypt, was on display. She wore it at the 1939 wedding of her daughter and Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, the future shah of Iran, according to the museum.
The thieves managed to get a hammer past security and used it to smash the glass case, grab the jewels and flee, police said.
The museum’s surveillance system caught the whole thing on camera, police said.
The Vienna State Police Directorate is asking the public to help identify the culprits, whom it described as slim men with dark hair and short beards.

The experts interviewed by NBC News said the Vienna robbery is the latest in a string of high-profile heists that have hit European museums, including the theft in October of French crown jewels and other items valued at $101 million from the Louvre in Paris.

“The thieves didn’t disguise themselves perhaps because they knew camera placement and quality,” Amore said. “With the advances in security technology, I fear we might see thieves turn to brute force more frequently in the future. Museums must prepare themselves for this, because they are all targets.”
Wittman said top-notch museum security requires good equipment, good guards and good procedures.

“It’s like a three-legged stool,” he said. “One leg goes and the stool tips over. Obviously, in this case, they didn’t have good human resources. I mean, the thieves were able to grab the necklace and get away.”
That having been said, Wittman said he’s confident the robbers will be found. He’s not so sure about the fate of the necklace.
“I expect it won’t take long before they know who they are,” he said of the thieves. “Hopefully, they’ll catch them before they melt this piece down.”

title: Death toll in Nepal floods tops 900; number of missing nearly doubles to more than 4,200
summary: Rescuers continue to struggle to reach communities days after the massive flooding that stemmed from a glacier collapse.
story: More than 900 people were killed by the devastating flooding in Nepal, officials in the South Asian country said Monday as the number of those listed as missing almost doubled to 4,247, including 592 foreign nationals.

The government “has mobilized all available resources and efforts at its disposal for search, rescue, and relief and recovery operations,” a spokesperson for the Nepali Foreign Ministry told a news conference Monday, before thanking a number of countries, including Qatar, the United Kingdom, Australia and Japan, for helping out with relief efforts.
“So far, 903 bodies have been recovered,” the spokesperson said, adding that 10,000 people had been rescued, including 323 foreign nationals.
Separately, Nepal’s disaster agency said 4,247 people were missing as of 1 a.m. ET Monday. On Saturday, the country’s foreign minister, Shisir Khanal, put that figure at 2,400.

title: Bootleg ‘Spider-Man’ swings into Russian cinemas despite Hollywood boycott
summary: While screening the movie “violates both Russian and international law,” everyone, including Russian authorities, “turns a blind eye to it,” one film critic told NBC News.
story: “Spider-Man” fans dressed up as their favorite web-slinger have swung into cinemas across Russia to see the latest installment of the franchise, despite Sony Pictures ending all of its theatrical releases in the country at the start of the war with Ukraine.

Wearing a homemade costume with the iconic spider symbol drawn onto a red shirt, Almir, 27, was among the hundreds who flocked to the cinema to watch “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” in the city of Kazan, which sits around 500 miles east of the capital, Moscow.
“I did it myself, since I didn’t have money for a full suit,” he told NBC News in a Zoom interview last week, adding that demand for tickets was so great that he had to book three weeks in advance.

NBC News agreed not to use Almir’s last name and those of other moviegoers because they were nervous about potentially landing themselves in trouble with authorities for speaking to a foreign media organization.

But while screening the movie “violates both Russian and international law,” everyone, including moviegoers, owners and even Russian authorities, “turns a blind eye to it,” according to the film critic Timur Aliev.

“Formally, a cinema has no right to screen a film without a distribution certificate,” Aliev said. But these were impossible to obtain, as most of the major Hollywood studios had closed down their distribution offices in Russia after the start of the war, he said.
